bio.en: Tomer Cohen is LinkedIn's longtime Chief Product Officer, piloting the 'Full Stack Builder' program that lets anyone take products from idea to launch regardless of function.
bio.zh: Tomer Cohen 是 LinkedIn 任职已久的首席产品官（CPO），他正在推行“全栈构建者（Full Stack Builder）”计划，让任何人无论职能都能将产品从想法推进到上线。

summary.en: Tomer explains LinkedIn's Full Stack Builder program, which scraps the traditional APM track in favor of an associate builder path where people from any function take products from idea to launch. He discusses why this broadens the talent pool, creates a new career ladder, and reflects on leading product at LinkedIn's scale. The episode is a forward-looking model for how companies may organize product building in the AI era.
summary.zh: Tomer 解释了 LinkedIn 的“全栈构建者”计划：它废除了传统的 APM（助理产品经理）通道，代之以一个“副构建者”路径，让来自任何职能的人都能将产品从想法推进到上线。他讨论了这为何能拓宽人才池、创造新的职业阶梯，并反思了在 LinkedIn 这种规模下领导产品的体会。本期是关于企业在 AI 时代可能如何组织产品构建的、前瞻性的样板。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: When we look at the skills required to do your job, by 2030, it will change by 70%. So whether or not you're looking to change your job, your job is changing. In order to stay competitive, you actually have to go back to some first principles, go back to the drawing board and reimagine what it means to be building.
turns.zh: 若以2030年为节点，回顾当前从事的工作，所需技能将发生70%的变革。无论你是否打算换工作，你的职位都将面临变革。若想保持竞争力，你必须回归基本原理，重新构想产品开发的本质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're experimenting with a very different way of building product at LinkedIn that fully embraces what AI unlocks.
turns.zh: 在领英，你们正在尝试一种全新的产品开发模式，充分发挥了人工智能的潜力。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: We call it the full stack builder model. The goal itself is to empower great builders to take their idea and to take it to market, regardless of their role and the stack and which team they're on. It's really fluid interaction between human and machine.
turns.zh: 我们称之为全栈构建者模式。其核心目标是赋能优秀的构建者，将他们的创意推向市场，无论其角色、技术栈或所在团队如何。这是人与机器之间高度流畅的协作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This feels like this could be a model for how a lot of companies operate and how product ends up being built in the future.
turns.zh: 这种模式或许能为许多企业的运作方式以及未来产品开发模式提供借鉴。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Change management here is going to be a critical part, but it's not enough to give them the tools. You have to build the incentives programs, the motivation, the examples to how you do it. I see a lot of companies roll out their agents and just expecting companies to adopt. It doesn't work this way.
turns.zh: 变革管理至关重要，但仅提供工具是不够的。还需建立激励机制、注入动力，并提供成功范例。我发现许多公司推出协作工具后，期望员工自然接受，但这种方法往往行不通。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: It really starts with kind of the basics. For me, technology has always been about empowerment. It's not about what it does for us. It's about what enables us to do. And now we have this amazing opportunity in my mind to make it about meritocracy, and I think it's an opportunity, but it's also a necessity right now, and I want to put this in context where we're entering this phase where the time constant of change is far greater than the time constant of response. Basically means that change is happening faster than we're able to respond to it. Now, LinkedIn has this unique view of the world of work. So we actually have some pretty, in my mind, mind-blowing stats to put this in perspective. When we look at the skills required to do your job, by 2030, which is literally four years from now, sounds a long time, but four years from now, it will change by 70%. (00:06:25): So whether or not you're looking to change your job, your job is changing. The only question is, do you keep it? And then we look at organizationally, the fastest growing jobs right now, the most in demand jobs in the market are growing by north of 70% from last year's fastest growing job. So there's a new kind of iteration of what you need as an organization to thrive. And then you apply that to building products and you realize that in order to stay competitive, you actually have to go back to some first principles, go back to the drawing board and reimagine what it means to be building. And what I love about this is when you think about the role of a builder, which the builder is at the heart of company, the goal is actually quite simple. The builder takes an ADN, she brings it to life. That's really the process, right? (00:07:11): And we all build those, let's call them best practices. You research the problem really well, you spec it out, you design it, you code it, you launch it, and you iterate. That's basically it. But what happens at many at scale companies, LinkedIn included and many other companies, over time that process became very complex very quickly. So what happened? We took every step and we expanded it to a lot of sub-steps. Researching, the problem became looking at for us 10 to 15 sources of information, obviously talking to customers about doing data pools, looking at feedback tickets in multiple sources, social media, interactions with customers. We probably have 10 to 15 sources of information we go for before we feel like we have research department really, really well. (00:07:58): Think about reviews for product. There is design reviews, privacy reviews, security reviews. I can go on and on and on. And each one of those substeps actually has a valid reason to exist. But when you add a whole thing together, you're like, "Oh my God. This is why it takes, to build a small feature, multiple teams, multiple code bases, multiple sprints just to get it out to launch," and not talk about iterating, which is actually where you seek success. You never see success in the launch itself. So really the work itself is not complex, but the process we made very complex. And when I was digging in, I found it doesn't end there because somebody has to do all those substeps, so what happened is you actually move from process complexity to organizational complexity as well. (00:08:41): And then you actually led to microspecialization. All those subsets are doing by somebody specific. So from one builder, we have multiple functions. Obviously we have engineering, product and design, and you can start questioning those lines. At least I am internally. And from there, we have a lot of subspecialties. It happens in every one of those functions, but imagine design. We have interaction design, animation design, content design, research. There's so many aspects to that. So they're all valid, but they all have people, and that entire process basically means a lot of... It's basically bloating. It's complexity. And then without noticing, you end up with this massively complex... We actually have this diagram that basically shows the process complexity, organizational complexity together. (00:09:26): And usually people are mind blown because they're working on one thing very specific, but when you zoom out, you have this overwhelming experience you're kind of thinking about. And now we have this real opportunity to collapse the stack backup, go back to craftsmanship, rethink the product development lifecycle, which is where the full stack builder model comes to life.
turns.zh:
这一切实际上始于一些基础层面的东西。对我而言，科技始终关乎赋权。重点不在于它能为我们做什么，而在于它能让我们做什么。如今，我们迎来了一个绝佳的机遇——将其与精英管理体系相结合。我认为这既是机遇，也是当下的迫切需求。正如我所说，我们正步入一个时代，变革的速度远超应对变革的速度。基本而言，变化的速度比我们能应对的速度快得多。

LinkedIn对职场的独特洞察为这一观点提供了有力佐证。就职场技能而言，到2030年（距离现在仅四年时间，看似遥远，但实则近在咫尺），所需技能将发生70%的变革。无论你是否打算换工作，工作本身都在不断变化。唯一的问题在于，你是否愿意坚守现有岗位？再看组织层面，增长最快的职位需求与去年相比增长了70%以上。这意味着组织要想蓬勃发展，需要重塑自身架构。将这些理念应用于产品开发时会发现，要想保持竞争力，必须回归基本原则，重新构想产品的构建逻辑。

我深切认同构建者的角色——构建者是企业的核心，其目标本质上很简单：将抽象概念转化为现实。基本流程是：深入研究问题，制定规范，设计方案，编写代码，发布产品并持续迭代。但在大规模企业（包括LinkedIn在内）中，这个流程逐渐变得极其复杂。究其原因，我们将每个步骤细化为无数子步骤：研究问题时要查阅10到15个信息源，与客户沟通数据池，分析多个反馈渠道的数据，监测社交媒体互动……最终耗费大量精力才完成初步研究。

产品评审环节亦是如此：设计评审、隐私审查、安全审核……每个子步骤都有其存在的合理性，但当它们堆积如山时，开发者会感叹：“天哪，开发一个小功能竟需要多个团队、多个代码库、多个冲刺周期才能上线”，更遑谈迭代优化——真正的成功往往诞生于迭代过程，而非发布本身。

归根结底，工作本身并不复杂，复杂的是我们自设的流程。深入剖析后发现，这不仅体现在流程层面，更延伸至组织层面。微型专业化趋势愈发明显：每个子领域都由专人负责，导致原本单一的构建者角色被多重职能分割。
我们有很多子专业领域。这种情况在每个职能部门都存在，但以设计为例。我们有交互设计、动画设计、内容设计、研究等领域。这其中包含诸多维度。这些专业方向本身都合理存在，但每个领域都需要专人负责，整个流程最终会导致……体系过于臃肿、结构过度复杂。不知不觉间，你就会陷入一个极其复杂的局面……实际上，我们有一张图表，清晰展示了流程复杂度与组织结构复杂度的关联。（00:09:26）通常人们会被眼前具体的工作所局限，但当你跳出局限，就会迎来令人惊叹的视野。如今，我们迎来了一个绝佳的机会——精简技术栈，回归工艺本质，重新审视产品开发全生命周期，而这正是全栈开发者模式大放异彩的时刻。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah. To be fair, there was always a change, right? So it was never about just keep the skills you have today, but we've never seen such a dramatic part of your role today. So whether you are a marketer right now or a seller, a recruiter, an engineer. Engineering is where a lot of the investment is going in right now in terms of agents. Those jobs will change dramatically. I remember I said my role, my life as an engineer and even then it's changed materially after 10 years, and then the change we're seeing right now, just thinking about in four years, what did it take to actually engineer really, really well would be dramatically different, or to build software, to build an artifact of some sort. But it's true for almost every function. It's not equal. Some job like nurses will see less impact, but some jobs will see 90%, 95% impact.
turns.zh: 是的。说实话，一直都有变革，对吧？所以这从来不是说要保留你现在拥有的技能，而是我们从未见过如今职位角色的变化如此剧烈。无论你现在是营销人员、销售人员、招聘人员还是工程师——工程师领域目前正吸引着大量投资。这些职位将发生巨大变革。我记得我曾说过，10年后我的工程师角色已发生重大变化，而如今我们所见证的变化更是惊人。比如四年后要想真正精通工程技术，所需的技能将与现在截然不同——无论是构建软件还是某种产品。但几乎每个职能领域都是如此。变化程度不尽相同。比如护士受到的影响较小，但有些职位的变化幅度高达90%、95%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's also a stat that I don't think you mentioned here that I saw on the post when you first talked about this program is that 70% of today's fastest growing jobs were not even on the list of jobs a year ago.
turns.zh: 我记得你在首次谈论这个项目时，帖子中提到一个数据：如今增长最快的职位中，70%一年前甚至不在就业榜单上。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah. No, so this is the fastest growing job on the list were not there a year ago, and then many of them don't even exist a decade or two ago. There's actually some pretty amazing stats across the board.
turns.zh: 是的。没错，这些榜单上增长最快的职位一年前根本不存在，甚至有些职位在十年前或二十年前还不存在。总体而言，相关数据着实令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So let's talk about this program that you built. Tell us the name and then tell us the gist of what it is today and the vision of where you want it to be.
turns.zh: 好的。那让我们来聊聊你开发的这个项目。先告诉我们它的名称，然后概述一下它目前的核心功能以及你的未来愿景。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah. So we call it the full stack builder model. And the goal, always start with the goal. The goal itself is to empower great builders to take their idea and to take it to market, regardless of their role and the stack and specifically which team they're on. And the idea ultimately is to be able for that builder is to develop experiences end to end, to combine skills and expertise across what was traditionally distinct domains to bring it all together. And it's not a sequence of steps. It's really a fluid interaction between human and machine. That's how the way I see it. And then when you look back at that product development life cycle from the idea, the insight all the way to launch, the key trait that I'm emphasizing for builders is where I want them to spend their time is where I think great builders should shine in. (00:12:54): So the idea of vision. Coming up with a compelling sense about the future. Empathy, super critical, right? Having a profound understanding of an unmet need. Communication is critical. And we see this a lot in job descriptions right now for almost every role, but ability for you to align and rally others around an idea. Creativity, which for me is about coming up with possibilities beyond the obvious. For example, I don't think AI yet is great at creativity. I think it's kind of, in many ways, brings back the things you might not know about, but it's not the kind of next level creativity, which I think still humans are much better at. (00:13:33): And then ultimately what I think is the most important trait for a builder is judgment. Some people call it test making, but it's making high quality decisions in what is complex ambiguous situations. Everything else, I'm working really hard to automate. Really, really hard. And then when you think about the outcome, it's not just about having more shots at the goal, which I think people go like, "Oh, the iteration speed is going to be very high." Yes, but what you're really doing to an organization of at scale organizations is they're a lot more nimble, a lot more adaptive, a lot more resilient. They can navigate the future. They can actually match the pace of change to the pace of response. (00:14:13): And an analogy I have in mind is kind of Navy SEALs. You come to training, they're all kind of learning, they're cross-trained, across multiple areas. What they specialize in is the mission and they operate in small pods and they're very nimble and you can assemble them very quickly. And I think that's going to be the organization that will win in the future.
turns.zh:
是的。所以我们称之为全栈构建者模式。目标始终要从目标开始。目标本身就是赋能优秀的构建者将他们的想法推向市场，无论他们处于什么角色、负责哪个环节，特别是在哪个团队。最终的目标是让这些构建者能够端到端地开发体验，将传统上分离的领域中的技能和专业知识结合起来，形成一个整体。这不是一个步骤序列，而是人与机器之间流畅的互动。这就是我的理解方式。当你回顾从构思、洞察到最终上线的产品开发周期时，我强调的关键特质是，构建者应该把时间花在他们最擅长的领域。

（00:12:54）：所以首先是愿景。构想一个引人注目的未来图景。同理心至关重要，对吧？深刻理解未被满足的需求。沟通能力也极为重要。我们现在几乎在所有职位描述中都能看到这一点，但关键在于你能否围绕一个想法团结他人。创造力对我来说意味着超越显而易见的可能性。我认为目前人工智能在创造力方面还不够出色。在很多方面，它只是挖掘出你可能不知道的东西，但还达不到更高层次的创造力，我认为人类在这方面仍更胜一筹。

（00:13:33）：而我认为构建者最重要的特质是判断力。有些人称之为测试制定能力，但它是指在复杂模糊的环境中做出高质量决策。其他一切，我都在努力实现自动化。真的非常努力。当你考虑结果时，关键不在于增加尝试次数——人们可能会说“迭代速度会很高”。是的，但你真正为大规模组织带来的好处是它们更加灵活、适应性更强、更有韧性。它们能驾驭未来，能与变化的速度同步。

（00:14:13）：我想到的一个类比是海豹突击队。接受训练时，他们需要跨领域学习。他们专攻任务，分成小队行动，非常灵活，组建起来也很快。我认为这样的组织才能在未来胜出。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So the simple idea, if you're just to boil it down to a sentence, the idea here is there's a builder who goes through the entire product development process essentially on their own. They have an idea, they research, they do data, they prototype design ship. That's kind of like the vision of where this goes?
turns.zh: 好的。所以简而言之，如果用一句话概括，这个模式的核心是构建者基本上要独自完成整个产品开发过程。他们有想法，进行研究，收集数据，设计原型，发布产品。这就像是展望未来的愿景吧？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yes, but it doesn't have to be on their own. It's not like... I still believe in teams.
turns.zh: 是的，但不一定要独自完成。不是说……我仍然相信团队的重要性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So smaller teams.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以是小团队。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Just smaller teams. Smaller teams and much more focused on the problem, the mission, per say, versus... Actually, one of the things we've done as an example, we started to do the idea of pods. We're no longer large teams. We assemble a team, ideally a full stack builders coming together and it's less about can I have an engineer design PM working together and trying to combine this trio looking at folks who can flex across and then they tackle something for a quarter or so and then we reassemble those two different pods. That's one example of an manifestation we're doing right now and seeing actually some great success in both in terms of velocity, but also in terms of that focus and nimbleness of that team.
turns.zh: 只是规模较小的团队。规模较小的团队更加专注于问题和使命，举个例子，我们现在推行的分组模式（pods）。我们不再组建大型团队，而是集合一批全栈开发者，重点在于让工程师、产品经理和设计师协同工作，组成灵活的团队。每个团队专注于某个季度内的特定项目，完成后再重组团队。这只是我们目前实践的一个例子，成果显著——不仅提升了开发效率，还增强了团队的专注力和灵活性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it feels like the goal here, what you're trying to adjust and that broke as teams bloated as speed and adaptability and flexibility, because going back to your original point that change is happening so much more quickly now that companies that have been building in this traditional way just can't compete.
turns.zh: 看起来你们的目标是调整现有模式，因为传统的团队结构导致速度和灵活性下降，无法应对快速变化的市场环境。正如你之前提到的，当前的变化速度太快，传统模式的公司已然无法竞争。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah. It's not that you have to break the model. I think the model is broken. It's just this pace of change is helping us realize it.
turns.zh: 是的。不一定需要彻底打破现有模式，而是要适应变化的节奏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So then going back to the things that these builders still do versus what you want to automate. So the list you shared is they're responsible for the vision, empathy, communication, creativity, and judgment.
turns.zh: 好的。回到这些开发者仍需承担的任务与你们希望自动化的部分。你们提到的清单包括愿景、同理心、沟通、创造力和判断力。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yes. Yeah. And I would put a lot of the focus on the latter. I think if you ask me at the end of the day, what's the kind of most important trait? I would say it's that judgment, test making ability.
turns.zh: 没错。重点在于后者。如果要说最重要的特质是什么？我认为是判断力和测试能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then in terms of what you're automating, what are some of the areas you've seen a lot of success in actually automating and where do you think this goes?
turns.zh: 那么在自动化方面，你们在哪些领域取得了成功，又认为这项工作将如何发展？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah. So I think just to kind of break it to pieces, and I think this is... If you were a startup right now, in many ways you can start this way. There's no legacy code, there's no legacy structure you run. And in fact, a lot of the startups I talked to that are built AI natively, they're just working at full stack builders. That's the way they start. If you're at a company at a scale of ours and many others in the market, you're like, this is almost like a new production function and mindset that you have to do. And there's really three components that we're working on. One is platform. The second one is the tools and the agents. And lastly is the culture. (00:17:17): The platform one, this is the kind of level of investment you have to do before, before this actually starts, you start to see all the benefits accrue. But the platform for us as an example is rearchitecting all of our core platforms so AI can reason over it. So we're building kind of this composable UI components with server side that we actually build. We're basically building for AI to be ready to bring it in. So you can't just go and bring a third party tool and have it work on the LinkedIn stack. In fact, that's one of our biggest learnings. It never works. Never works. You have to bring it in and customize a lot of it, working almost in alpha mode with those companies to make it work internally.
turns.zh: 是的。简单来说，如果是初创公司，可以直接采用这种模式，没有遗留代码和结构需要处理。但对于像我们这样规模的公司和市场上的其他企业来说，需要逐步转型。这主要涉及三个方面：平台、工具和文化。（00:17:17）首先是平台投资，必须先进行重构，才能享受全部好处。但以我们为例，重构核心平台是为了让AI能在其上进行推理。我们构建了可组合的UI组件和服务端架构，为AI的接入做好准备。无法直接引入第三方工具并在LinkedIn系统上运行。这是我们最大的教训之一，效果永远不理想。必须深度定制，与合作伙伴以测试模式共同开发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this is essentially re-architecting your code base to work more efficiently with AI. Is that one way to think about it?
turns.zh: 因此，本质上就是要重新架构你的代码库，使其能更高效地与人工智能协同工作。这是理解这一点的思路之一吧？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yes. And in many ways, working with those companies to adjust something in their stack to work with our stack as well.
turns.zh: 是的。在很多方面，我们与这些公司合作，调整他们的技术栈，使其能与我们的技术栈兼容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you say those companies, meaning the development agents like Cursors and [inaudible 00:18:16] and such?
turns.zh: 你说的这些公司，是指像 Cursors 和 [音频不清晰 00:18:16] 这样的开发平台之类的吗？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yes. Or Figma on design. Or you can think about design systems is another example of that. But you have to have that back and forth because they're not... In many ways, we haven't seen anybody be able to work off the shelf immediately on our code-based design systems and unique context we have.
turns.zh: 是的。或者在设计方面，Figma 也是一个例子。但你必须反复沟通，因为他们并不能……在很多情况下，我们还没看到有任何公司能直接把我们的代码化设计系统和我们独特的上下文无缝对接。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to follow that thread briefly, so there's Figma. That's interesting. So basically the way Figma exports and keeps your design system, that has to change to work better with AI is what I'm hearing.
turns.zh: 稍微总结一下，所以有 Figma。这挺有意思的。所以基本上 Figma 导出并维护你的设计系统的部分，需要进行调整才能更好地与人工智能协同工作，这就是我听到的情况。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: They first need to know how to work with our design systems, which is something, in many ways a lot of those companies are working on. Same with coding. It doesn't work that you just bring it in and it just reasons over your code base really well. We tried. We are building that layer that basically allows it to do so, whether it's Copilot or Cursor, Windsurf and so on.
turns.zh: 他们首先需要了解如何与我们的设计系统协同工作，这在很多方面是很多这些公司正在努力解决的问题。编码方面也是如此。不是说你把它引入进来，它就能完美地解析你的代码库。我们尝试过，但我们正在构建一个层级，基本上能让它做到这一点，无论是 Copilot、Cursor、Windsurf 还是其他工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. Oh yeah, Copilot. Microsoft. I get it. I get it. Okay. Okay. So that's the platform. So that's an investment that you guys have to make to make AI effective at building and doing all these things.
turns.zh: 明白了。好的。哦，对，Copilot。微软。我懂了。懂了。好的。所以这就是平台。这是你们为让人工智能能有效地构建和做所有这些事情而必须进行的投资。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: And then you have tools. So tools is where you really build the agents. I mentioned I want to automate everything outside of those five trades that we talked about, and then we're building the tools for that. And then for that, actually very similarly, I can't just bring a tool from the outside and work. So I'll give you an example. One of our biggest things is building a trust agent. Trust is really important for us at LinkedIn. There's a lot of unique vectors which trust plays at LinkedIn doesn't place it anywhere else. So we need to bring all of that know how and context and information base into that agent. So we ended up building our own trust agent at LinkedIn.
turns.zh: 然后还有工具。工具才是真正构建智能助手的地方。我提到过，我们想把除了我们谈到的五个行业之外的所有事情都自动化，然后我们正在为此构建工具。同样，在工具方面，我们也不能直接引入外部工具就能完美适配。举个例子。我们最重要的工作之一是构建信任助手。信任对我们 LinkedIn 来说非常重要。信任在 LinkedIn 发挥作用的很多独特维度，在其他地方都找不到。所以我们需要把所有这些专业知识、上下文和信息库都整合到这个助手中。所以我们最终在 LinkedIn 构建了自己的信任助手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so what is this trust agent doing? Telling you when you're maybe exposing information that you shouldn't be?
turns.zh: 那么这个信任助手是做什么的？比如提醒你可能正在泄露不该泄露的信息？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: So when you build a spec, you build an idea, you walk through the trust agent and it'll basically tell you what are your vulnerabilities, what harm vectors potentially you're introducing or will be introduced as a result of that. And I had our head of trust build it. So the head of craft for every area is building their own agent. As an example, we have one of our features for job seekers is called Open to Work. If you're looking for a job, you can put an open to work.
turns.zh: 所以当你构建一个规格说明书、一个想法时，先让信任助手过一遍，它会基本告诉你有哪些漏洞，可能会引入或即将引入的危害向量。信任助手是由我们的信任主管构建的。所以每个领域的工艺主管都在构建自己的助手。举个例子，我们有一个面向求职者的功能叫“Open to Work”。如果你正在找工作，可以在上面填写“Open to Work”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, a little green loading thing on the circle.
turns.zh: 是的，圆形图标上有个绿色加载提示。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Exactly. And actually it's a great signal. I've seen some great success from it. People are helping each other. The community really thrives around helping each other. But at the same time, it introduces a trust vector for bad actors because they're open to work. People who are looking for a job are potentially more vulnerable to scams than other folks. So being able to think about how do we prevent all of those ahead of time. So we walked that spec from a couple of years ago through the trust agent. Not only was it able to find all the stuff we initiated at the beginning, but all the holes that we did not catch until later. So that's a great example of something that actually worked really well. (00:21:03): That's one. The other one is a growth agent, as an example. Again, LinkedIn has a very unique... Actually, we have an incredible growth team, growth process. We've kind of funneled all of our unique loops, our funnels, our tests of the past, everything into this growth agent, and now you can basically rock your respect for it, your idea for it. And it would not just allow you to do it better. It would actually critique how good is your idea. This is something you cannot bring off the shelf. It's very unique to LinkedIn. So we had to invest dramatically in it. And one team which is using it right now, which is almost... I wasn't thinking about it at the beginning, but our UXR team, our UER team, the user research team is usually using that growth agent to understand out of all the things that are basically surfacing for members, which one has the biggest growth opportunity to have the biggest impact? That was not in the cards when we thought about that idea, but teams are basically funneling those ideas into this one. (00:22:05): An example is our research agent. So research agent basically is trained on the personas of our members. You can think about a small business owner, a job seeker and so on. And it's using not just world knowledge, it's using all the research we've done in the past, all the support tickets coming in. So it's pretty good at understanding that persona at LinkedIn. So one examples we had is a team came out with a spec. They weren't aware we had the research agent yet. I asked the research agent for a small business owner, wanted to think about the marketing spec we had, and it critiqued it extremely well. Actually, in many ways shifted the direction of the team to focus on other integrations tools we can focus on, but it's very hard to have that visibility all to all that corpus of knowledge inside of the company. (00:22:56): That's another example. We have an analyst agent trained on all how you basically can query the entire LinkedIn graph, which is enormous. And instead of relying on your SQL queries or data science teams, you can use the analyst agent. All of those I would say are, I would call them still MVP+. The goal for us in the next couple of months to basically roll them out externally. Externally, I mean, internally at LinkedIn.
turns.zh:
确实如此。这其实是一个很棒的信号。我从中看到了很多成功案例。人们相互帮助，整个社区因此而蓬勃发展。但与此同时，它也为不良行为者带来了信任漏洞，因为这些人乐于接受工作机会。正在找工作的人比其他人更容易遭遇诈骗。因此，我们需要提前思考如何预防这些问题。几年前，我们将那个方案引入信任代理模块。它不仅能发现我们最初设想的所有问题，还能找出后来才发现的漏洞。这就是一个非常成功的例子。

（00:21:03）：还有一个例子是增长代理。同样，LinkedIn拥有非常独特的……实际上我们有一个出色的增长团队和增长流程。我们把过去所有的独特循环、漏斗和测试都整合进了这个增长代理，现在你可以充分利用它，发挥你的创意。这不是现成就能用的东西，它对LinkedIn来说非常独特。因此，我们在此方面投入了大量精力。目前有一个团队正在使用它，几乎……我最初并未考虑到这一点，但我们的用户体验研究团队（UXR）和用户体验设计团队（UER）通常会利用这个增长代理，了解会员们反馈的所有信息中，哪些具有最大的增长潜力和影响力。这在我们构思这个想法时并未考虑到，但各团队正将这些想法整合到这个平台中。

（00:22:05）：再举一个例子，研究代理。研究代理主要基于我们会员的用户画像进行训练。你可以想象一个小企业主、求职者等等。它不仅利用常识，还整合了我们过去所有的研究成果和收到的支持工单。因此，它能相当准确地理解LinkedIn上的这些用户画像。比如，有个团队提出了一个方案，他们当时并不知道我们已经开发了研究代理。我让研究代理分析一个小企业主的营销方案，结果它给出了非常好的反馈。实际上，在很多方面，它甚至改变了团队的方向，让他们转向其他集成工具。但在公司内部，要全面掌握这些知识库实在太难了。

（00:22:56）：还有一个例子。我们有一个分析代理，经过训练，它可以查询整个庞大的LinkedIn图谱。与依赖SQL查询或数据科学团队不同，你可以直接使用分析代理。我想说，这些都可以被称为MVP+版本。我们的目标是在未来几个月内将它们推向外部市场。外部市场，我指的是LinkedIn内部。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not as new product lines.
turns.zh: 不是新产品线。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So many questions. One is just how are you building this? Is there a platform you're using? What does it take to build an agent at LinkedIn? Is it all internal tools or is there third party use?
turns.zh: 好的。问题太多了。首先是你们如何开发这些产品？你们使用的是什么平台吗？在LinkedIn开发一个代理需要什么？是全内部工具还是会使用第三方工具？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: It's a great call. So I think we've been experimenting with a lot of tools. And I would say for a lot of those kind of knowledge corpus agents, we're using everything from Copilot Enterprise to ChatGPT Enterprise. By far though, the most important part was basically our own customization of it. That's been where we saw the biggest gains. Even building the orchestrator across those because you want the agents to start following to each other, the trust agent should work with the growth agent and go do a back and forth versus doing what more sequentially. So we've done a lot of work internally to make it happen. This is why I think it does require that level of investment. (00:24:09): And then in some cases, let's talk about the design agent that we're working with. We're working with multiple companies to try and understand which product works best for us. And interestingly enough, and this is another learning, different teams gravitate to different products. So that's something we'll have to resolve and think about how we do this really well, because ultimately we were trying to simplify the process as much as possible, but that was a big learning for us and which tools we use and how we basically integrate them in.
turns.zh:
这真是个明智的决策。所以我认为我们一直在尝试各种工具。对于许多这类知识库智能助手，我们使用了从Copilot Enterprise到ChatGPT Enterprise的各种产品。但到目前为止，最重要的部分还是我们对它们的深度定制。这才是我们取得最大成效的地方。甚至在跨产品协同方面，我们也下了很大功夫——因为你希望这些助手能够相互协作。例如，信任助手应该与增长助手配合，形成良性循环，而不是各自为政。所以我们内部做了大量工作，才实现了这一目标。这就是为什么我认为这确实需要大量投入。

（00:24:09）：再说说我们正在合作的设计助手。我们与多家公司合作，试图找出最适合我们的产品。有趣的是，这是另一个经验教训——不同团队对不同产品的偏好各不相同。这是我们需要解决的问题，要思考如何才能把这件事做得更好。毕竟我们的初衷是尽可能简化流程，但这对我们来说是个沉重的教训，涉及到我们使用哪些工具，以及如何将它们有效整合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So you might have an amazing Figma agent, but some teams want to use a different design tool.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以你可能有很棒的Figma助手，但有些团队想用其他设计工具。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah. So we've kind of experimented with Figma and Subframe and Magic Patterns and so on, and we saw people gravitating depending on the function, their level of visibility, their know how of the tool before, they're gravitating to different tools. And ultimately, I don't want to have eight design agents in the company, so we have to converge into at least a few. And I think it's similar across many areas because the appeal of those, a lot of those agents are trying to solve similar end goal, but they're doing it very differently. And what you'll see that ultimately, I don't think there's going to be a winner takes all because the starting point of the customer or the user will dictate a lot how simple they are for that use case.
turns.zh: 是的。我们尝试了Figma、Subframe、Magic Patterns等工具，发现人们会根据功能、可见度、之前对工具的熟悉程度等因素选择不同的工具。最终，我不想在公司里部署八个设计助手，所以我们必须整合到至少几个统一的助手中。我认为很多领域的情况都类似，因为这些助手的吸引力在于它们试图解决相似的最终目标，但实现方式却大相径庭。最终，我认为不会出现赢家通吃的情况，因为客户或用户的起点将极大地影响这些助手在特定用例中的易用性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super interesting. The other interesting takeaway here is you're designing very specific agents that are one job to be done. Is that a very intentional decision? Did you try an agent that just is super intelligent on all these things?
turns.zh: 非常有趣。另一个有趣的启示是，你们设计的都是专注于单一任务的特定助手。这是一个刻意的决策吗？你们有没有尝试过一个在所有这些方面都超级智能的助手？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Ultimately, they will do an orchestrator. We're going to really orchestrator across, but we did want to be able to rate and grade those agents really well on how they're doing. And I think there is a level of expertise. Now, we're kind of building this in a way where we'll be able to mask a lot of those. You might not know that there's a trust agent. You might have, we call this internally the product jammer agent that basically does your product jam, which is a process we do internally. You might just use the product jam engine, and that product jam agent will work with all the other agents. But now we're starting with that building blocks until we build the orchestrating layer across.
turns.zh: 最终，它们会形成一个协调机制。我们确实会进行跨产品协调，但我们确实希望能够对这些助手的表现进行有效评级和分级。我认为这需要一定的专业知识。目前，我们正在构建一个框架，通过它可以掩盖很多复杂性。比如，你可能不知道有信任助手的存在。我们内部称之为产品阻塞助手，它主要负责我们的产品阻塞流程（这是我们内部的一个流程）。你可能只会使用产品阻塞引擎，而这个产品阻塞助手会与其他所有助手协作。但现在我们从这些基础模块入手，逐步构建跨产品的协调层。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another interesting takeaway from what you've been sharing is that so much of the work has gone into the beginning of the product development process, just like helping you craft the right requirements, clarify trust, and then here's product jam and here's the research we've done. And I imagine it's because coding has already been accelerated with all these IEE tools. Talk about just why that's maybe where most of the investment's gone and where you've seen the most impact so far.
turns.zh: 你们分享的内容中另一个有趣的点是，产品开发流程的初期阶段投入了大量精力——比如帮助团队制定合理的需求、明确信任关系，还有产品研讨会，以及我们所做的研究。我想这可能是因为借助了这些 IEE 工具，编码工作得以加速。能否谈谈为什么大部分投入都集中在这一阶段，以及目前取得的最大成效？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Well, 100% our coding investment has gone, started a while back, and those are fall into place. We have our coding agent. In fact, we've kind of staged it into two parts of it. There is the idea to design part, and then let's call it the code to launch part. The code to launch part has gotten a lot of attention and we're making some big inroads there. Everything from the coding agent to what we call the maintenance agent when you have a failed build, it will do it for you. In fact, I think we're close to 50% of all those builds being done by the maintenance agent and a QA agent.
turns.zh: 是的，我们 100% 的编码投资都投入其中了，这项工作早在之前就已经启动了。现在各方面都已步入正轨。我们有编码代理，甚至将其分为两个部分：设计阶段和上线阶段。上线阶段目前备受关注，我们在这方面取得了重大进展。从编码代理到维护代理（当构建失败时会自动处理），所有环节都实现了自动化。事实上，目前约 50% 的构建任务都是由维护代理和 QA 代理完成的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. So this is when a break builds instead of engineers hopping on the issues that an agent fix.
turns.zh: 哇。所以这就像是让代理来处理问题，而不是工程师亲自去解决。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: You can still go and finish your coffee before you have to go and redo the build again.
turns.zh: 这样你就能先去喝咖啡，之后再重新构建代码。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Extremely cool.
turns.zh: 太酷了。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: But we haven't had much investment until we kind of launched this program in the idea to design area. And that's a material part of work. It's also where the quality a lot of the work comes from, at least before you start to go into the coding phase. The idea is to empower everybody. So if you're an engineer, you can basically use all those tools at the front of the process and be able to be a full stack builder.
turns.zh: 但在启动这个设计领域的项目之前，我们并没有投入太多资金。这部分工作至关重要，也是保证质量的关键环节，至少在进入编码阶段之前是如此。我们的目标是赋能每位成员。工程师们可以利用前期准备的所有工具，成为全栈开发者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How long did it take to get this kind of in place for you to actually form your first team to build these, the initial agents and some of this backend, redo the code base sort of thing?
turns.zh: 你们花了多长时间搭建起初始团队，开发这些代理、后端系统以及重构代码库？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: I announced this internally end of last year, we really kind of started working, but it was more setting up the teams and the processes internally. We had our first MVPs of those agents I think like four to five months after it was really trained, I would say. But really the work itself has been kind of couple of months of dedicated work. A lot of it has been getting all the corpus of data together, cleaning it up. And that's actually a good learning as well. It's not great to just give it access to your drive and say, "Reason all over this knowledge base." It actually does a very poor job understanding importance of the past and putting weights on stuff. You actually want to think about specifically what the context when do you want to give it to and what's the knowledge base that you want to have it focused on. So even cleaning up, let's call them gold examples or golden examples to learn from, has been one of the biggest learnings. Just reasoning over your entire knowledge base did not work.
turns.zh: 去年底我在公司内部宣布了这个项目，但实际工作主要集中在团队组建和内部流程搭建上。第一个 MVP 版本在经过四到五个月的深度训练后才推出。真正的工作核心是持续几个月的专注投入，包括整合数据集、进行数据清洗。这其中最大的收获之一是，不能直接让系统访问你的文件夹并声称能理解整个知识库。实际上，系统对过去数据的重要性理解得很差，无法准确赋予权重。必须明确在何时、以何种知识库为中心提供数据支持。这甚至包括清理数据集——我们称之为黄金样本——以此作为学习素材，单纯对整个知识库进行推理是行不通的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that makes sense. There may be just like a researcher with a strong opinion about something that you disagree with and it wouldn't know. It's like, oh, of course, this is data, this is fact.
turns.zh: 是的，这说得通。可能会有研究人员对某些观点固执己见，而开发者却不以为然。比如，他们会觉得“这就是数据，这就是事实”。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Exactly. And then it doesn't always understand ties to original specs to success. You have to actually build... This is a really interesting way. When you think about how you bring those tools in, you can't just bring them in. You have to know what you feed them with. And what you feed them with is not just access. I see a lot to just focus on the connectivity and integration and it reminds me of the... This is almost like, this is actually more than 10 years ago when I was co-rebuilding the team, co-rebuilding the feed at LinkedIn and we started from scratch and I had to literally sit down and filter through examples of what is a good professional post on LinkedIn and what is not. And this was like weeks of work getting up that golden sample of examples, but it wasn't... The most important part was feeding at the right data, not all the data. (00:29:57): So it requires work. This is where I would say for many companies who are thinking about this phase, and I do a lot of sessions today with CPOs and COs on this process. You have to put this initial work to get the gains after. When I think about it, I think there's a takeaway there in generally with AI, even if you're learning it for the first time and so on, whether it's Cursor or whether it's design, if it's Figma or other tools or Lovable, you should be ready to invest those hours before you start seeing yourself pick up in velocity and quality, which will come up, but you have to invest that time.
turns.zh: 确实如此。而且它并不总是能理解与原始规格相关的成功因素。你必须实际去构建……这是一个非常有趣的方法。当你思考如何引入这些工具时，不能简单地直接引入。你必须清楚为它们提供什么样的数据输入。而这些数据输入不只是接入问题。我看到很多人只关注连接性和集成，这让我想起……这几乎就像，十多年前我在领英（LinkedIn）重新组建团队、重建信息流时那样。我们从零开始，我不得不亲自筛选并整理什么样的内容才算优质的领英专业帖子。这项工作花了好几周时间，但成果并不显著……最重要的部分是提供正确的数据输入，而不是所有数据。（00:29:57）：所以这需要付出努力。对于许多正处于这一阶段的公司，我要说——今天我和许多首席产品官（CPO）及首席运营官（COO）一起探讨了这个过程。你必须先投入初期工作，才能在之后收获成果。回想起来，我认为这在人工智能领域有一个普遍的启示。即使你第一次接触人工智能，无论是Cursor、Figma还是Lovable等工具，你都应该准备好投入大量时间，才能看到自己的工作效率和质量得到提升，而这些提升终将到来，但你必须先投入时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Miro. Every day, new headlines are scaring us about all the ways that AI is coming for our jobs, creating a lot of anxiety and fear. But a recent survey for Miro tells a different story. 76% of people believe that AI can benefit their role, but over 50% of people struggle to know when to use it. Enter Miro's innovation workspace, an intelligent platform that brings people and AI together in a shared space to get great work done. Miro has been empowering teams to transform bold ideas into the next big thing for over a decade. Today, they're at the forefront of bringing products to market even faster by unleashing the combined power of AI and human potential. Guests of this podcast often share Miro templates. I use it all the time to brainstorm ideas with my team. Teams especially can work with Miro AI to turn to unstructured data like sticky notes or screenshots into usable diagrams, product briefs, data tables, and prototypes in minutes. You don't have to be an AI master or to toggle yet another tool. The work you're already doing in Miro's Canvas is the prompt. Help your teams get great work done with Miro. Check it out at miro.com/lenny. That's M-I-R-O.com/lenny. (00:31:46): What's the current state of the pilot? How large is it? How many teams are doing it? What kind of stuff have you shipped? Just give us a sense of today's world.
turns.zh: 本期节目由Miro赞助。每天，关于人工智能将抢走我们工作的头条新闻都让我们感到恐慌，引发了诸多焦虑和担忧。但Miro最近的一项调查却揭示了不同的情况。76%的人认为人工智能能为他们的工作带来益处，但超过50%的人不知道何时该使用它。Miro的创新工作空间是一个智能平台，它将人和人工智能聚集在一个共享空间中，共同完成出色的工作。十多年来，Miro一直在助力团队将大胆的想法转化为下一个重大创新。如今，他们正站在前沿，通过释放人工智能和人类潜力的协同力量，更快地将产品推向市场。本播客的嘉宾经常分享Miro模板。我经常用它和团队一起头脑风暴。团队尤其可以借助Miro的AI，将便签或截图等非结构化数据在几分钟内转化为可用的图表、产品简介、数据表和原型。你无需成为AI专家，也无需切换另一个工具。你在Miro画布中正在进行的工作本身就是提示。用Miro助力你的团队完成出色工作。请访问miro.com/lenny。（00:31:46）：试点项目目前处于什么阶段？规模有多大？有多少团队在参与？你们已经推出了哪些成果？请给我们一个当前的概况。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah. I wouldn't say we are yet at a very high sample rate where it's kind of a high percentage of the organization, but we have a substantial part of the organization already using it to provide a lot of the feedback. We're seeing a lot of great examples. So the way I think about the benefits is a function of experimentation volume multiplied by quality. How good are those experiments divided by the time it takes to actually pull them out, like idea to launch. So on saving times, we're seeing, whether it's PMs, designers, engineers, saving hours of work a week right now, whether it's the analyst agent we talked about or the prototyping really quickly or the product jamming experience has been a big part of that. On the quality side, we're seeing insights discussions just be much, much better. And by the way, quality and time, sometimes they help each other because it's high quality, you don't have to spend as much time on something. (00:32:52): So we are seeing that applied in. And the volume, I wouldn't say we had a rate where I'm seeing a high percentage organization doing it yet, but this will come once we... We haven't GA'd this internally. That will come in the next couple of months once we have all the stuff in place. But we're seeing designers and PMs picking up bugs directly from Jira tickets, pushing them in, something we haven't seen before, and there's just an appetite for everybody to just join. So in fact, the biggest thing right now is everybody wants access. Everybody wants access to the tools to be able to do it together, and we just want to make sure it's good enough to make sure the whole organization can do it really well.
turns.zh: 是的。我不会说我们目前的采样率已经很高了，覆盖了整个组织的很大一部分，但我们已经有相当一部分员工在使用它来提供大量反馈。我们看到了很多优秀的案例。所以我认为其带来的好处取决于实验的数量和质量。这些实验的质量有多高，以及从构思到上线实际花费的时间有多短。所以在节省时间方面，我们看到无论是产品经理、设计师、工程师，现在每周都能节省数小时的工作时间；无论是我们提到的分析师角色，还是快速原型设计，抑或是产品冲刺体验，都起到了重要作用。在质量方面，我们看到洞察讨论的质量有了显著提升。顺便说一下，质量和时间有时是相辅相成的——因为质量高了，就不需要在某些事情上花费太多时间。（00:32:52）：所以我们已经看到了这些应用。至于数量，我不会说我们已经有很高比例的组织在使用它，但一旦我们……我们内部还没有全面推广。但接下来几个月，一旦所有条件都到位了，我们就会推广。我们看到设计师和产品经理直接从Jira工单中提取缺陷并提交，这在以前是从未有过的，而且大家都渴望加入进来。事实上，目前最大的问题是每个人都想获得访问权限。每个人都想获得工具来共同协作，而我们只想确保工具足够好，能让整个组织都能很好地使用它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So how is it that you're piling it? Is it some number of people have access to these agents and they just work the way they've worked with access to these tools? Or is there a team dedicated, this is the way you work now and this is it, and we'll see what happens.
turns.zh: 那么你们是如何推广它的呢？是让一部分人访问这些工具，然后他们就按照之前的习惯工作吗？还是有专门的团队，现在就是这样工作方式了，然后看看效果如何。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: So that's a great call. So basically we have a team building. It's the core team building the FSB track across all of R&D, FSB, full stack builder. And then there are pockets and pods of teams using it. So basically we are looking at specific areas that we're basically giving it to. The condition there is they give feedback. As a response for that, they make the tool better, so it's not just access. We want people who will use it. So one of your early adopters would be the ones who help [inaudible 00:34:15] up the product really well. So we're doing this in a pod model right now.
turns.zh: 这真是个好主意。基本上，我们有一个团队在建设。核心团队在研发、FSB、全栈开发等各个领域建设FSB流程。然后还有一些团队的小组在使用它。所以基本上我们正在针对特定领域进行推广。前提条件是他们要提供反馈。作为回应，我们会改进工具，所以这不仅仅是访问权限。我们希望人们能够真正使用它。所以早期采用者之一应该就是那些能很好地帮助提升产品质量的人。所以我们现在采用的是小组模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's like a pod within a larger team, like a designer, PM, engineer kind of group within... Is there an example? You have a part of LinkedIn that's trying this out?
turns.zh: 所以这就像一个大团队中的小组，比如设计师、产品经理、工程师之类的团队……有没有例子？LinkedIn有哪个部门在尝试这个吗？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah. So if I think about some of our teams, whether it's... Actually, we just launched Semantic People Search and the Semantic Job Search as well. That team was using part of those tools to actually help build it. So that team actually, this was PMs building their own dashboards with those tools without waiting for design resources to come in. Then we have a design team who is now... This started really from the manager rolling this out. And in many ways, what I tell this team is, "Don't wait for the official GA. Start doing it. Start leaning in." We're seeing designers of that team starting to push PRs, which never happened before. And now other teams, they want to do this as well. So it's starting with this kind of grassroots experience. I would say the places have been very formal. I would say the beginning has been the top. (00:35:22): The product executive teams, basically we move from functional leaders, design, PM, BD, and so on to product areas leaders, and they basically rock across the stack and they also go for a 360 with all of those functions to see if they're really able to do a full stack building experience. Then we're also launching at the junior side a new program called the Associate Product Builder Program, where basically we used to have our APM program, which this is about it's ending this year. And then starting January, we're going to start having our APB program and they're going to come into LinkedIn. We're going to teach them how to code, design and PM at LinkedIn. They're going to go through a pretty rigorous training process, and then they're going to join those pods, and gradually we're going to grow that program to be a material part of LinkedIn as well.
turns.zh: 是的。所以如果我看看我们的一些团队，无论是……实际上，我们刚刚推出了语义化的人员搜索和职位搜索功能。那个团队正利用部分工具来实际搭建这些功能。所以那个团队实际上——这是产品经理们自己用这些工具搭建仪表板，而无需等待设计资源到位。然后我们有一个设计团队，现在……这实际上是从经理推动项目开始的。在很多方面，我对这个团队说："别等正式上线了。开始行动吧。积极参与进来。"我们看到那个团队的设计师开始提交 PR 了，这在以前从未发生过。而现在其他团队也想效仿。这种自下而上的经验正在兴起。我得说，以前我们的流程非常正式。最初是由高层主导的。（00:35:22）：产品执行团队基本上是从职能部门领导、设计、产品经理、商务拓展等转向产品领域领导，他们全面掌握各个环节，并与所有职能部门展开全方位合作，验证自己是否能具备全栈式产品开发能力。然后，我们在初级层面推出了一项名为"初级产品构建者计划"的新项目。之前我们有 APM 项目，今年即将结束。从明年1月起，我们将启动 APB 项目，参与者将加入 LinkedIn 团队。我们将教他们如何在 LinkedIn 进行编码、设计和产品管理。他们将经历严格的培训过程，然后逐步加入各个小组，最终使这个项目成为 LinkedIn 的重要组成部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. So this might be the future of the APM program is this full stack builder APM-ish program.
turns.zh: 哇。所以 APM 项目的未来可能是这种全栈式构建者式的 APM 式项目。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: In many ways, we've built some pretty amazing... I'm really excited for that group. I wish I could join it. But we build amazing training for them. And in many ways, we're going to use that training to think about how we roll it across the organization. We're kind of using the lens of you have great technical skills, but you're not an engineer at a company yet, or you have great design taste, but you haven't designed at scale in company yet, and we're going to teach you how to do it at LinkedIn, but the training we're going to use a lot to extend across the company as well.
turns.zh: 在很多方面，我们已经打造了一些非常棒的……我对这个团队真的很兴奋。我希望自己能加入。但我们为他们提供了很棒的培训。很多方面，我们将利用这些培训来思考如何在整个组织中推广。我们以这样的视角来看待这个问题：你有很强的技术能力，但还不是公司的工程师；或者你有很棒的设计品味，但还没有在公司进行过大规模设计。我们将在 LinkedIn 教会你如何做到这些，同时也会大量利用这些培训在整个公司推广。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So you have these programs, these pilots and these pods, and you said what you're looking at to see if this is something you roll out is experiment velocity times quality times time.
turns.zh: 好的。所以你有这些项目、试点和小组，你说你想看看是否要推广，这个过程就是实验速度乘以质量再除以时间。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Divided by time.
turns.zh: 除以时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Divided by time. Okay.
turns.zh: 除以时间。好的。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. And I guess I know it's early, but just you said you're seeing that it's saving teams a few hours a week at this point, something like that?
turns.zh: 明白了。我想虽然现在还早，但你说目前这些项目已经为团队每周节省了几个小时的时间，是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah. And I think the feedback has been the most important part. Right? The way to think about this is just like you build a product. So we're building this product internally and you want to experiment with some kind of early adopters who will give you feedback, and the feedback has been amazing. In fact, our top talent are the ones who are using this the most at LinkedIn. And the feedback from them has been incredible in terms because they're also willing to spend the time and give the feedback as well. And the response from them has been incredible in terms of like the quality of their output, the time they're spending on this to get the value back, their desire to be part of this and actually scale this and make this even better. So that's where a lot of the excitement has been from how they're using it and the quality we've seen there. I would say in six months or so, we'll be able to see a lot more of the organization use it and you'll start seeing those top line numbers will build as well.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为反馈是最重要的部分，对吧？思考这个问题的方式就像你开发一个产品一样。我们正在内部开发这个产品，你想先让一些早期采用者进行测试，他们会给你反馈，而这些反馈令人惊喜。事实上，我们 LinkedIn 的顶尖人才是使用这个产品最多的人，他们的反馈也非常出色——因为他们也愿意花时间提供反馈。他们的反馈在输出质量、投入时间获取价值、渴望参与其中并进一步优化产品等方面都令人赞叹。这正是他们积极使用该产品以及我们所见证的卓越成果的来源。我认为大约六个月后，我们将能看到更多组织开始使用它，届时相关核心数据也会随之提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a really interesting insight that the top performers are finding the most success, because there's always been this question, is AI going to just make people that are not amazing, more amazing, or is it going to make amazing people even more amazing? And it sounds like it's likely the latter.
turns.zh: 顶尖人才能取得最大成功，这确实是个很有趣的见解，因为一直存在这样一个疑问：AI 会让表现平平的人变得更出色，还是会让优秀的人更加卓越？听起来很可能后者。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yes. And in many ways, it's surprising, it's not surprising. I've seen this also when we were... It's surprising because you want everybody else to be part of this and lean in. I think top talent has this tendency of continuously trying to get better at their craft and this innate need to be at the cutting edge of how you build, and I think we're seeing this here as well. This is why I had this phrase I say with the team that if we build all those tools, will they use it? And I know right now the answer is no. It's not enough to give them the tools to use it. You have to build the incentives programs, the motivation, the examples to how you do it. They need to see other people being successful as well. (00:39:11): And I've seen this also when we're shifting LinkedIn from a desktop company into a mobile company. It was a very similar process. It's very hard. Change management here is going to be a critical part. I think I see a lot of companies roll out their agents and just expecting companies to adopt. It doesn't work this way. Some will adopt. That tends to be your cutting edge 5% of talent that just wants new tools and they have a bias for change. But the vast majority needs to work for change management in how they do it, and that requires being a lot more thoughtful about the cultural aspect of it, which is by far from me the biggest and most important thing to do.
turns.zh: 是的。在很多方面，这既令人惊讶又不足为奇。我在我们内部开发产品时也观察到过类似现象。令人惊讶的是，人们都希望其他人能参与其中。我认为顶尖人才有不断提升自身技能的倾向，也有站在技术前沿的内在需求，我认为我们在这里也看到了这种情况。这就是为什么我对团队说的一句话是：如果我们开发了所有这些工具，他们会用吗？我知道现在答案是否定的。仅仅给他们工具是不够的，还必须建立激励机制、激发动力，并提供成功案例。他们需要看到其他人也能成功。（00:39:11）我还在将 LinkedIn 从桌面端公司转变为移动端公司时观察到过类似过程。这是一个非常艰难的过程。变革管理将是关键环节。我看到很多公司推出聊天机器人后，就期望所有人都能采用。这种方法行不通。有些人会采用，但这往往是5%渴望新工具、对变革有偏好的人。但绝大多数人需要在变革管理上下功夫，而这就要求我们更深入地思考文化层面的影响——这对我来说远是最重要和最关键的任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I want to spend time there. And it makes a lot of sense why people don't spend time here because they have so much to do. They got to ship things. Their days are already busy. You have to now carve out time to learn this new tool that'll not pay off for a while. So I get why people are like, "Okay, okay, I'll get there. I'll use it someday," but they don't. This idea of culture, when I saw you share this initially, this is the third piece of making this successful. So there's the platform of getting the code base ready for people for AI to work with. Then there's the tool, like the agents you've talked about, and then there's the culture. Is there more there that you can share of just what has actually worked in helping get people on board? One thing I heard is creating a little bit of FOMO of like, okay, only a few people can use this and you have to sign up to get access. What's worked in getting people to get on board?
turns.zh: 是啊。我想在那里待上一段时间。人们不愿花时间在这里（学习新工具）其实很有道理，因为他们要做的事情太多了。他们得发货，日常工作就已经很忙了。现在你还要抽出时间去学习这个新工具，而短期内又看不到回报。所以我理解人们为什么会说：“好吧好吧，我会慢慢学的，总有一天会用上的。”但他们往往并未付诸行动。关于文化这块，当我最初看到你分享这个观点时，我觉得这是成功的第三个关键要素。首先是搭建好让AI开发者能用的代码库；然后是工具层面，比如你提到的智能助手；最后是文化建设。能否再分享一些具体的成功案例？我听说有个策略是制造一点紧迫感，比如只让少数人能用这个工具，需要注册才能访问。具体怎么做才能让大家积极参与呢？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah. I think this is where I emphasize to people that getting everything done, the platforms, the tools is not going to be sufficient. It's a prerequisite for this to work, but not sufficient for this to work because it really requires you to invest a lot in the cultural aspects of how do you get people to lean into this one. And this one might feel slow at first, but I've seen this before with our transformation of thinking from desktop to mobile. And once it picks up, it actually maintains very high velocity. One, people are really incentivized by how you define expectations for them. So to think about what is the expectation of somebody in the role, whatever-
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这就是我要向大家强调的：光是搭建好平台和工具是不够的。这些是成功的前提，但远远不够。因为真正要让大家积极参与，你得在文化层面下大功夫。比如刚开始可能会觉得进展缓慢，但我见过从桌面端向移动端转型的例子。一旦大家适应了，进展就会非常快。首先，要让大家清楚自己的角色期望。比如——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So like changing performance review sort of things.
turns.zh: 比如调整绩效评估机制之类的。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Very much so. So everything from how you hire to calibration and evaluation. And one thing I want to see there early is this kind of AI agency and fluency. Like I mentioned, the tools are there. The question is, would you use them? Because the tools will be good enough, but not great at the beginning. That's the classic thing of every good MVP tool. They're good enough, but they're not great. And then you kind of want to build that agency to make the tool better. We're in this kind of notion of we're going to make this better for LinkedIn together. Two is piloting success inside of your organization. That's the pod model where you're showing that not only this could work, it's actually having success. So we have even our partnerships team, our BD team, being able to go instead of relying on waiting for an engineer to help build the developer portal and build the connectors there. (00:42:17): Literally one of our head of partnerships just went and did it himself. Didn't even delegate to his team. And their goal is to say like, "Hey, I can do it. You can do it as well." Those examples are really, really powerful. I talked about the associate product builder program where we are going to be very focused on training. I think that will send a really strong message across the organization. People will see this talent and what they can do, and I think that will create that movement. But celebrating wins in all hands, highlighting people and showing those examples. One example we've seen recently, people really looked at it in a surprise lens, but then it kind of, I think, really opened up a lens for them. We had somebody in our user research team. We had an opening for a PM on the growth team, and that role was open for a while, and she said that, "I think I can do it." (00:43:11): And she used all these tools. This is a user researcher becoming a growth PM, not usually the career path you see, but she was excited about the area. She used all those tools, and she's now a growth PM on the team. And really, you can start thinking about her more as a full stack builder ultimately. But seeing those openings and then highlighting those two people, actually people who are doing this have been a great example of it. And then just making sure that those tools are accessible. People can provide feedback, you share a lot, has been an incredible part of this. It's not enough to be top-down directive that this is how we want to work. People want to feel like there are success stories. They feel like it's worth their time. It feels it's a movement they want to be part of, and then ultimately they can see successes in how they do it.
turns.zh: 确实如此。从招聘到校准和评估，方方面面都要考虑到。我希望尽早看到的是那种人工智能代理和熟练应用的能力。我之前提到过，相关工具已经存在，但起初它们还不够完善。这是每个优秀MVP工具的典型特性——它们足够实用，但尚未达到卓越水平。然后你就需要建立这样的团队来优化工具。我们秉持这样的理念：我们将共同为领英打造更优质的体验。第二点是，在你的组织内部试点成功案例。这就是pod模式——你要展示出这种方法不仅可行，而且已经取得了实际成效。比如我们的合作伙伴团队和业务拓展团队，现在能够直接操作，而不必等待工程师来搭建开发者门户和连接器。（00:42:17）：实际上，我们的合作伙伴团队负责人刚刚亲自上阵，没有把任务交给下属。他们的目标是说：“嘿，我能做到，你也能做到。” 这些例子非常有说服力。我提到的初级产品构建者项目，我们将重点放在培训上。我认为这将在整个组织中传递出一个强有力的信号。人们会看到这些人才的潜力和他们的能力，我相信这将引发一股变革浪潮。但要确保所有人都能庆祝胜利，突出优秀员工并分享成功案例。最近我们就看到一个例子，人们对此感到惊讶，但随后我认为这为他们打开了一扇新视野。我们用户研究团队有一位成员，增长团队有一个职位空缺已经很久了，她说：“我觉得我能胜任这个角色。” （00:43:11）：她用上了所有这些工具。这位用户研究员成功转型为增长PM，这通常不是常见的职业路径，但她对这个领域充满热情。她运用了所有这些工具，现在已经成为团队中的增长PM。说真的，你可以把她视为全栈型人才。通过展示这些成功案例，突出这两个优秀员工，人们就会深受鼓舞。让这些工具易于使用，鼓励大家提供反馈，大量分享经验，这些都是关键之举。光靠自上而下的指令来强制推行新工作方式是不够的。人们需要看到成功案例，感受到这值得他们投入时间，他们会觉得这是一场值得参与的变革，最终他们也能看到自己的成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this kind of comparison to the shift to mobile. We all went through that and there's all these stories of companies requiring you to show mobile mocks. That's the only way we're going to operate. Now everything you have to ship has to be on mobile, and it's interesting how similar this is to them, to that experience. And so a few things you just shared here just to kind of summarize some of the things that have worked for you. Showing wins, celebrating wins, showing people what other folks are doing with AI tools, creating a program that people enroll into and make it a little bit exclusive. This performance review piece is really interesting because that really will change people's behaviors. Here's how we get promoted. Have you actually already made that change to the PM? I guess it's every track, I imagine, not just product management. Have you already made that change or is it kind of like a work in progress?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢把这比作向移动端的转型。我们都经历过那个阶段，记得那些公司要求展示移动端模型的故事吗？那就是我们现在必须遵循的路径。现在所有要交付的产品都必须支持移动端，整个过程与他们的经历惊人地相似。接下来你分享的几点总结了你们成功的关键：展示成果、庆祝成功、向大家展示其他人如何运用AI工具，以及创建一个独家参与的绩效评估项目。这个绩效评估环节真的很重要，它能真正改变人们的行为。告诉他们晋升的标准是什么。你们已经在产品经理团队中实施了这些改革吗？我猜不只是产品管理部门，其他部门也应该在推进这些变革吧？你们已经完成了这些改革，还是仍在推进中？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: So there was two aspects to it. Once I moved my team, my directs, we did 360 for them. So their 360 was, if you came from PM, you had the designers on your team rate you. And so that had its own, and then we shared those with them, and that had its own kind of motivation. But then we broadly took it across. So when we hire right now, we look for those. And then this upcoming cycle, we do a bi-annual. That's going to be part of the performance evaluation piece and we announce it to everybody. And for what, it's where people are excited to show. And they're excited to know how they're going to be... It's always about, like, "I want to know how I'm being rated or evaluated." So just being able to show those examples has been a big part of it. (00:45:31): The other thing I would say, it takes time for this program and its formality to roll out across the entire organization, and I was intentionally not trying to be quick at rolling this out to everybody because I think that just dilutes the value of it really quickly because it's not about... I could care less about your title. I care about how you work. So calling you a full stack builder is not what I'm looking for. Changing your mindset to a full stack mindset is what I'm looking for. You're thinking you can do the whole thing. You're looking at those tools and looking at how to do it. (00:46:07): So one of the things I've said is if you're looking for a formal reorg or declaration to start building differently, you're waiting too long. Look, my biggest thing is here's a permission for me to just not wait and just go. So whether or not you have the right tools or not, go build the tool, use a tool from the outside, bring it in, show those examples. In many ways, prove that you are a full stack builder in mindset before anything else come to mind. And that just naturally will happen, and that's also where we've seen some of our best talent just goes and leans a lot into.
turns.zh:
这里有两个方面。首先，我把团队迁到新部门后，给他们做了360度评估。如果你从产品经理岗位转来，团队里的设计师会给你打分。这种评估有其自身的激励作用，之后我们还与他们分享了评估结果，同样起到了激励效果。接着我们将其推广到整个组织。目前招聘时，我们会寻找具备这些能力的人才。下一个评估周期，我们将进行半年度评估，这将成为绩效评估的一部分，并向全体员工公布。人们对此充满期待，迫切想展示自己的成果，了解自己的评分标准。关键在于能够展示这些成功案例。

(00:45:31): 还有一点，这项计划及其正式化流程在全公司推广需要时间。我故意不急于快速推广，因为这样会很快削弱其价值。这不是关注你的头衔，而是关注你的工作方式。所以称你为全栈开发者并不重要，重要的是你能否转变为全栈思维模式。你要相信自己能独立完成整个项目，研究相关工具并付诸实践。

(00:46:07): 我曾说过，如果你等待正式的重组或声明才开始以不同方式构建团队，那就等得太久了。关键在于，我允许大家不必等待，直接行动。无论你是否有合适的工具，先去构建工具、使用外部工具、引入工具，展示成功案例。在很多方面，先从思维上证明自己是全栈开发者，其他方面自然会随之而来。这也是我们看到许多优秀人才主动投入的关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I was going to actually mention that quote. Someone you shared, you work with told me exactly that quote you just shared, so I'm glad you brought it up of just if you're waiting for a reorg, you're not thinking about it the right way. How do you encourage people to actually play with these tools on their own? Are you just like, "Go take a few days to play with AI?" Is it just try it? Or is there anything formal you've seen of just getting people to more try this on their own without joining this program?
turns.zh: 我很赞同这一点。我正想提及你分享的那句话。某位与你共事的人曾向我准确引用了你刚刚分享的这句话，所以很高兴你能提到这一点——如果你在等待重组，那说明你没有正确看待问题。如何鼓励人们主动尝试这些工具？你们是否会直接说“花几天时间玩玩AI吧？”还是采取更正式的措施，比如让人们在不加入正式项目的情况下自主探索？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: A lot of the tools we've made, we've been sharing them regularly. A few of my all hands have been all about how to use those tools. But then at the same time, we're kind of inviting, have you found a new tool that works really well for you? Share it, show it. Again, it could be Slack, could be Messages, Teams and so on, how you do it. But the idea is really to start getting that investment in how things work. Actually, I think in general, you can feel overwhelmed by tools right now, by recipes and how to do things like what's your prompt and what's my prompt. But really it's finding something that kind of works really well, that can gravitate around and really invest in that's been those areas. But I think we've had this invitation to go and explore and go and bring in stuff that you think are great. And in many ways, bring others along on the journey. It's one good way to make the influence much bigger than a few folks who are doing really well with this.
turns.zh: 我们开发的许多工具一直在定期分享。我的几次全体会议都是关于如何使用这些工具的。但与此同时，我们也在积极邀请大家：你是否发现了某个特别好用的工具？快来分享并展示吧！无论是Slack、Messages、Teams还是其他工具，只要你能讲清楚使用方法就行。但最重要的是，要真正投入到工具的使用中去。我认为总体而言，大家现在可能会被各种工具、操作指南和使用技巧搞得应接不暇，比如“你的提示是什么？”“我的提示又是什么？”但关键在于找到真正好用的工具，并深入研究和应用这些工具。我觉得我们一直在鼓励大家去探索和引入自己认为优秀的工具，并带上其他人一同前行。这是让影响力远超少数优秀个体的有效途径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any surprises on the negative side that have come out of this, of PRD is just feeling like AI driven, people slowing down unexpectedly? Is there anything that surprised you of just like, "Okay, this is actually not great"?
turns.zh: 在负面方面，PRD项目有没有出现什么意外情况，比如人们对AI驱动的工具反应迟缓？有没有什么让你们感到惊讶、觉得“哦，这其实并不理想”的情况？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Yeah, we mentioned a few of them. I was hoping for some tools to work off the shelf really well. It was never the case because we had to invest quite a lot.
turns.zh: 是的，我们提到了几个例子。我原本希望有些工具能直接上手，但事实并非如此，因为我们投入了大量精力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Never the case.
turns.zh: 确实不是这样。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Never the case. We had to invest quite a lot. And again, part of it is we just have a lot of legacy information and code based and knowledge and designs and so on. So a lot of the companies we work with are seeing this as a great growth opportunity for them as well to invest, but I do think it's a big area of investment as well. We talked about not just giving access to all of your context which we started with, and we were like, "Oh, here's access to all the drive, all information," failed miserably and hallucinates like crazy." People gravitating towards different tools, like our goal was to converge on tools, but that was pretty hard. (00:48:58): And then I think in terms of quality, we've just seen better quality, but I think it's because, again, where we are in the stage is still the early adopters and they're doing a few iterations in terms of how to do it. But I would say the tooling adoption is hard. And then I think for some people, this is important for me to kind of state, some people do not want to be full-stack builders, and that's completely okay. Some people see themselves in specialization, and I think specialization has a place and a role. So I didn't want the message to be across the organization I expect everybody to be a full-stack builder. I do not. I think there are system builders that empower full-stack builders, and then you have people who are specialized. But I don't think we need as many specialized people as we did in the past.
turns.zh: 确实不是这样。我们投入了大量精力。再说了，部分原因是我们有大量遗留的信息、代码、知识和设计等。所以很多合作公司也把这视为一个绝佳的增长机会，愿意投入资源，但我认为这确实是一个需要大量投入的领域。我们谈到过不只是开放所有上下文——我们最初就是这么做的，结果惨不忍睹，人们疯狂地寻找其他工具。我们的目标是统一工具标准，但这实在太难了。（00:48:58）然后在质量方面，我们确实看到了进步，但我认为这是因为我们目前还处于早期采用阶段，他们还在不断迭代操作方法。但我要说工具的采用确实很困难。然后我觉得有些人需要明确一点，有些人不想成为全栈开发者，这完全没问题。有些人专注于某个领域，我认为专业化也有其存在的价值和意义。所以我不想传达一个信息，要求整个组织里的每个人都成为全栈开发者。我不这么认为。我认为有一些系统构建者能够赋能全栈开发者，然后还有一些专注于某个领域的人。但我认为我们不需要像过去那样那么多专注于某个领域的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't actually realize this until just now. So is this their title now instead of product manager engineer, they're full stack builder?
turns.zh: 我直到现在才意识到这一点。所以现在他们的职位名称不再是产品经理工程师，而是全栈开发者了？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: We have a full stack builder title formally inside the organization, and we are gradually putting people in that bucket.
turns.zh: 我们在组织内部正式设立了全栈开发者职位，并且正在逐步将人员归入这个类别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So there's a whole career ladder that's forming. There's a whole... Okay. That's a bigger deal than I even thought. So where are you finding these folks mostly coming from, like product, engineering, design? I imagine it's a mix, but just is there a most common trend?
turns.zh: 因此，整个职业晋升通道正在形成。这……好吧。这比我想象的要重要得多。你主要从哪些部门招来这些人才，比如产品、工程、设计？我猜是多种来源，但有没有最常见的趋势？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: It's a mix. People listening, I would just think about just go over your org and imagine who can do it, who can right now flex across those functions, whether it is engineering, design, product, even BD, and what you'll find is there's already quite a few that can flex across.
turns.zh: 确实是多种来源。听众朋友们，你们可以回想一下自己的团队，思考谁能胜任这些跨职能的工作，无论是工程、设计、产品，甚至是商务拓展（BD），你会发现已经有不少人能够跨职能协作了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. Are there any functions you think are especially successful at this? Not to play any favorites, but I don't know. Are you finding like, okay? Or you could also not highlight any specific.
turns.zh: 有意思。你觉得哪些部门在这方面特别成功吗？不是说偏袒哪个部门，但我也不确定。你有没有发现某个部门特别突出？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: No, I think it's a mental model of how you do it. I think if I were to play what's the hardest craft to potentially learn, I think design has a lot more work to get the design agents to be really, really good. So I think designers have a little bit of a leg up in terms of others learning their craft than the vice versa. But I honestly think it's a mindset. I've seen designers code, I've seen PMs kind of design and do well. And this is why I think when you kind of step back and you think about people in your organization and who can flex, I think you'll see them show up in many areas. And what I think you'll find there is they have the agency, they're leaning into new things, they have the fluency, like they're already building new experiences and they have that growth mindset that they just want to get better, so it doesn't matter what they learn at school or what label somebody put in them when they join the company.
turns.zh: 不，我认为这是一种思维模式。若要说哪个职业最难掌握，我觉得设计师要真正成为优秀的设计师，需要付出更多努力。所以设计师在学习其他技能方面可能稍占优势，但说实话，这更多是心态问题。比如我见过设计师写代码，见过产品经理参与设计并做得很出色。这就是为什么我认为，当你退后一步，审视组织中能跨职能协作的人才时，你会发现他们在多个领域都有出色表现。关键在于他们有行动力，乐于尝试新事物，思维灵活，能够创造新体验，还有成长型思维，始终渴望进步。无论他们在学校学过什么，或是加入公司时被贴上什么标签，都无关紧要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I love about a lot of this is it's the easiest time to transition between different product roles than it's ever been. Design's moving to PM, and sure, or just moving to this new role, it makes it so much easier to, like you said, that researcher became a growth PM.
turns.zh: 我最欣赏的一点是，如今不同产品角色之间的转换比以往任何时候都容易。设计师向产品经理转型，或者直接转向新角色，都比以往简单得多。就像你说的，那个研究员成长为增长型产品经理的例子。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: And this is probably my biggest advice slash motivation I give to the team because what I tell them is ultimately... By the way, this is for me as well. I think about it the same way. The incentives for you are so aligned with your organization of what we're asking for, right? Because we need you to change. We want to be a more agile, adaptive, resilient organization that can deal with the pace of change, but you want as well for your own career. You want to be at the cutting edge of how you build. So the incentives are really aligned between what you need for your own career and what the organization needs you to do. So there's that permission to go and do it for me is ideally kind of a tailwind in what they want to do more than anything else.
turns.zh: 这或许是我给团队最大的建议和激励，因为我告诉他们，最终……顺便说一句，这对我自己也适用。我也这么想。你的职业动机与组织的需求高度一致，对吧？因为我们需要你做出改变。我们希望成为一个更敏捷、更适应、更有韧性的组织，能够应对变化的步伐，但你自己也希望在职业生涯中保持领先。因此，你的个人发展与组织的需求紧密结合。这就为你提供了许可，让你去做这件事。对他们来说，理想情况下，这应该是一种顺风，推动他们去做更多事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe a last question for people that are inspired and like, "Okay, this is what we need to be doing," any just tips for someone starting down this road to be successful at trying something like this at their company?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题是，对于那些深受启发、想说“好吧，这就是我们需要做的事”的人，有什么建议给刚踏上这条路的人，让他们在公司成功尝试类似做法？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: I would say I would start with the notion of how do you want to bring this just structure. I would think about the platform you need to build, the tools you want to bring, and then I would spend a lot of time on the culture. Platform and tools I think would be, again, a prerequisite, but not sufficient, and the cultural aspect is really important. I would think a lot about how you bring people along. So for one of the learnings we had that probably able to do it differently right now, if I were to redo this program was, for a while I was working very closely with my core team on it, the core kind of full stack building team that were in charge of building all this material, but the organization was always asking questions. "What's going on? Who is doing it? What are the tools?" And in retrospect, we could have done a lot more in the flow to just show them and get them to already use early tools or be aware of it versus doing a small team on the side. (00:53:49): So it's okay to start with a small team. I think it's really important. But at the same time, just making sure there's visibility across the whole thing is really powerful. Being patient and being willing to invest. I always give this example of, we always give this example of like, "Oh, look at this startup. They built this in a week." Yes, you can build lifestyle in a week right now if you start from scratch. It's actually not hard. But when you are trying to transform a large organization, you want to have this impatient about the goal and you have to have a high ambition, but being very thoughtful and patient about how you bring it to life and the key things you have to invest in. If you don't invest in your platform, I just don't see how this could be a successful outcome. If you don't invest in customizing the tools for you, then you're just going to get vanilla generic agents from the outside. (00:54:39): So being aware of the investment and making sure you actually allocate resource to it, this is kind of the classic, be willing to invest upfront so you can reap the benefit after, versus saying, "Hey, why am I not seeing us moving into 2X the productivity in a week?" That's not going to be this way. You can see it with some people, but starting to collect those examples and starting to really think about the transformation is really key.
turns.zh:
我想我会从如何搭建这个合理架构的理念入手。我会思考你需要搭建的平台、引入的工具，然后花大量时间在文化建设上。平台和工具在我看来是前提条件，但仅有这些是不够的，文化层面至关重要。我会深入思考如何让团队跟上进度。在我们的经验中，有一点值得借鉴——如果现在让我重新规划这个项目，我可能会采取不同的做法。比如，我曾与核心团队紧密合作，带领这个全栈开发团队负责搭建所有材料，但组织层面总是在追问：“进展如何？谁在负责？工具是什么？” 回想起来，我们本可以更早地让团队参与进来，让他们尽早熟悉并使用新工具，而不是让小团队在一边单独操作。

（00:53:49）所以从小团队入手是没问题的，这非常重要。但同时，确保整个过程的透明度也至关重要。要有耐心，愿意投入资源。我常举个例子，比如“看这家初创公司，他们一周就做出了产品”。是的，如果你从零开始，确实能在一周内打造出生活方式类产品，这并不难。但当你试图改造一个大型组织时，必须对目标保持耐心和雄心壮志，同时要深思熟虑、耐心推进。若不投入平台建设，我实在看不到成功的可能性；若不为其量身定制工具，你只能从外部获取千篇一律的通用解决方案。

（00:54:39）所以，要意识到投入的重要性，确保资源到位。这是经典的理念——愿意前期投入才能收获后续回报。别抱着“一周内就能让生产力翻倍”的不切实际期望。有些人可能短期见效，但真正关键的是持续积累经验，深入思考转型路径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so incredibly cool. I know that a lot of CPOs and heads of product and all kinds of leaders are reaching out to you trying to figure out what you've learned how to do this. So I love that we went deep on all these things. Just final question, is there anything else that we haven't shared that you think might be helpful for listeners to hear or maybe just to double down on before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 这真是太棒了。我知道很多首席产品官、产品负责人以及各类管理者都在向你求教，试图理解你成功的秘诀。所以我很高兴我们能深入探讨这些问题。最后一个问题：有没有什么我们尚未分享的经验，你认为听众听了会受益，或者在我们即将开始的精彩闪电问答环节前需要再次强调的？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Whether you're in an organization, you're waiting for your leader to roll this out or you're a leader trying to roll this out, I would not wait. The first thing I've done, which I thought in retrospect was very hopeful is I did announce this upfront we are going to this mode. We're starting in pockets, we're starting in pods, we're building the tools, but this is the mountain we're going to go after, and in many ways, we're going to make it great. I also announced that this is not just an end state, it's a kind of continuous progress. There's no state we're going to get to as much as continuously just trying to be better. And in many ways, to compete, you just want to be better than others in how you build because the version of building will completely just transform itself every few years or so. (00:56:13): So do not wait. Really focus on the progress you're making, over communicate with your team, not just the vision, but also the progress you're making, almost like holding yourself responsible. If you're a leader, give yourself KPIs you share with your own teams or OKRs. And if you're inside of the organization, and I would say whether or not or not your CPO or your CEO is announcing this type of program, go do it or join an organization that does it so you can be at the cutting edge of how you build in the future.
turns.zh: 无论你身处某个组织，正在等待领导者推行变革，还是身为领导者正试图推动变革，我都建议你别再等待了。我首先做的，回想起来确实充满希望——那就是公开宣布我们将向这个模式转型。我们从局部试点开始，逐步推进工具开发，但这座山峰终将被我们征服。某种程度上，这不只是终极目标，更是持续进步的旅程。没有终极状态，我们只需不断努力超越自我。（00:56:13）所以别再等待了。真正专注于你正在取得的进展，与团队充分沟通——不仅要传达愿景，更要汇报实际进展，几乎像是对自己负责一样。如果你是领导者，为团队设定KPI或OKR。如果你身处组织内部——无论CEO或首席产品官是否宣布这类计划——主动行动起来，或者加入正在推行变革的组织，这样你就能站在未来构建的技术前沿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tomer, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 托默，接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有五个问题要问你，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题：你最常向他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: I love to give trios of books that I really like. So my current trio is, they're very diverse in topics, so apologies if it's not falling all into tech. But the first one is called Why Nations Fail. It's a book I read a decade ago even more and the authors of it just won the Nobel Prize last year. And it basically talks about why does some nations succeed and some fail? And it's not the usual explanations we go for, which is, oh, it's culture, it's natural resources, it's the kind of religion. A lot of those tends to be the kind of immediate excuses people have. It kind of falls into two camps. Are there extractive or inclusive institutions? Can people participate broadly and opportunities shared or there are institutions that basically are supposed to be attracting from many and give to some. (00:57:48): So it's just an incredible way to just think about how you build a nation. And for us at LinkedIn, we think a lot about the idea of opportunities, so how you build a product as well. And it's just a good way to move away from easy explanations into what really makes a country really successful as well. Second book, it's called Outlive. It's really about the idea, it's kind of like the author, Peter Attia talks about the idea of medicine 3.0, which is really the notion of building personalized medicine, which I think in the world of AI will become incredible in the future. But it's all those, let's call those categories that you should think about for your life so you can just optimize your health as much as possible and goes for everything through fitness to diet to the biggest health factors you should think about. But it's a great long book. Then lastly-
turns.zh:
我喜欢推荐三本我真心喜欢的书。现在我推荐的三本主题各不相同，抱歉可能不全是科技类的。第一本叫《国家为什么失败》。这本书我十年前读过无数遍，作者去年刚获得诺贝尔奖。书主要探讨为何有些国家成功，有些失败？这本书抛弃了常见的解释，比如文化、自然资源、宗教等简单借口。归根结底，关键在于两种制度：是掠夺性还是包容性机构？人们能否广泛参与，机会能否共享？还是说制度注定从多数人那里索取，却只惠及少数人？（00:57:48）这本书能让人深刻思考国家构建之道。在LinkedIn，我们深思机会的概念，以及如何打造产品。它帮助我们跳出简单解释，深入探究真正造就成功国家的要素。
第二本书叫《超越极限》。这本书核心观点是，作者彼得·阿蒂亚提出的医学3.0概念，即构建个性化医疗。我认为这在AI时代将迎来突破。书中涵盖了各类维度，比如健康优化，从健身、饮食到重大健康因素。但这是一本厚重之作。
最后一本——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The one in my bookshelf behind me.
turns.zh: 我身后书架上的那本。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 就这样吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's up top. You can't actually see it, I think.
turns.zh: 它在最上面了。我觉得你看不到它。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: And then lastly, it's a book that also came out many years ago, but it's called The Beginning of Infinity, which I really like, by Deutsche. It wasn't an easy read for me, but I love the idea. In fact, especially in products, I love the idea of cause and effect, like really finding great explanations for why things happen and then building on top of that your next iterations. And this book really pushes on the idea of explanations that only once we have a clear understanding of what things happens, then we can have breakthroughs on top of that. But until we get to a point of clear scientific breakthroughs, we are not going to make significant progress. But when you do that, it's really almost like infinite progress you can make on top of that.
turns.zh: 最后，还有一本书，也是很多年前出版的，叫《无限的开端》，我很喜欢，作者是德施特。对我来说，这本书读起来不算轻松，但我很喜欢其中的理念。特别是产品设计方面，因果关系的思维模式真的很棒——去找到事物发生的深层原因，再以此为基础进行迭代改进。这本书深刻探讨了只有在充分理解事物运作机制后，才能实现突破的观点。但在达成明确的科学突破之前，我们很难取得重大进展。但当你真正理解了这些原理，接下来的进步就几乎是无限的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Naval's always talking about that last book. I think I bought it and it was just hard reading this.
turns.zh: 内瓦尔老是提起那本书。我记得买过，但确实读起来很费劲。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: It's not an easy read, at least for me. It wasn't an easy read, but it's a very powerful read.
turns.zh: 这本书读起来不轻松，至少对我来说是这样。它确实很有深度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Is there a favorite recent movie or TV show you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最近有没有你特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: Can I do a podcast?
turns.zh: 我能做个播客吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 当然可以。

turns.speaker: Tomer Cohen
turns.en: So there's a podcast in, it's in Hebrew, it's called One Song, and it takes a song that generally is ideally popular and then goes really deep on the origin and the history of the song, and I love it. I love music and just dissects songs so well. It does a great job also in bringing to life the story behind it. So for me, it just goes back to you thought the song was about something, but then it goes really deep into the actors behind the song, and sometimes it's the words chosen or it's how the lyrics match the music itself, and I just really enjoy that one.
turns.zh: 有个播客叫《一首歌》，全是希伯来语的，它会深入剖析一首流行歌曲的起源和历史，我超爱的。我热爱音乐，它把歌曲剖析得特别透彻，还能生动呈现背后的故事。比如你以为歌曲讲的是某个主题，但它会深入探讨幕后创作者，有时是歌词的选择，或者旋律与歌词的完美契合，我特别喜欢这个播客。

turns.speaker: Lenny
